title: GroundTruth: what the ground knows about the week
note: The one source for both decks: the live deck (site/talk/) reads it, and presentation/story/build_pptx.cjs builds the PowerPoint from it. Numbers are never typed here: a static slide names a chart, and talk.js draws its numbers from data/*.json (written by src/presentation_data.py). beats.title: You shook the ground today
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Think about how you got to our University today. A car, a bus, the metro, or your own two feet. Every one of those pushed on the ground. A few billionths of a metre, far too small to feel, but real. So here's a question. What day is it today? Easy: you'd check your phone, or remember what you did yesterday. But how do you actually know? Mostly from what everyone around you is doing. Now imagine you had no phone and no calendar, only an instrument buried under the city, writing down every shake. Could it tell you what day of the week it is? That's our question. Here's one day of that writing.

Take a second. It was a Wednesday: Christmas Day, 2019. Our model said Sunday. In a few minutes you'll see why it was right to be wrong.

beats.title: Last time: one question
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Two months ago we asked one question: can a seismometer tell what day it is? We made five promises. Short answer: we kept all five, then kept going. So, what is it actually hearing?
beats.screen: A still: last time's question and the five promises.

beats.title: What a seismometer records
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: Every car, bus and footstep pushes on the ground and sends a tiny wave down through the rock. Down here is the instrument that catches it. A seismometer is a heavy weight on a spring. When the ground moves, the weight lags behind, and the instrument measures that difference. Seismologists built these for earthquakes, and everything else they call noise. Now watch one whole day. At night the city sleeps, and the pen barely moves. Hardly anyone is driving or walking. Then morning arrives. This is a real recording: an ordinary Wednesday, the fifteenth of January 2020, under Brussels. Quiet at night, a jump at around seven when people start moving, and high all day while the city works. In the evening it slowly falls again. That noise is a city waking up, working and going to sleep. Shraddha, who else has listened?

beats.title: Who listened to cities before us
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: We're not the first to study noise in cities. In 2017, a team in Barcelona connected city noise to traffic, the metro and crowds. (Next) During the pandemic, four years of recordings from Tokyo showed that weekday daytime noise returned quickly after the first state of emergency, while Sunday noise took longer to return. (Next) More recently, researchers have mapped city activity street by street using fifty kilometres of fibre-optic cable, as they did in San Jose.
beats.screen: Row 1: Díaz 2017, Barcelona.
presses: Row 2: Nimiya 2021, Tokyo
Row 3: Liu 2025, San Jose

beats.title: Where they stopped, and where we start
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: docs/02-data-and-sources.md, "Papers" and "Where this project goes beyond the papers"
beats.notes: So where did they stop? They mainly measured average patterns: over an hour, a type of day, or during a lockdown. We look at one day at a time, testing the model only on weeks it hasn't seen before. They focused on one city or one event, while we used 149 seismometers, then expanded to 33 cities over seven years, and tested the model on cities it hadn't seen before. (Next) Some studies needed phone data for comparison. Our model doesn't need that, and its own mistakes can help find holidays without being given holiday labels. Other researchers removed human activity to study earthquakes. We kept it as our main signal and also tested whether removing it could help detect earthquakes. It didn't, and we'll show you why. (Next) Some studies needed large sensor networks or new fibre-optic cables. We use seismometers already installed in the ground, and our system runs a test every night. Aradhya, where do our recordings come from?
beats.screen: Rows 1–2: averages vs one day at a time; one city vs 149 seismometers and 33 cities.
presses: Rows 3–4: phone data vs no phones; removing people vs keeping them
Row 5: dense arrays or fibre vs seismometers already in place

beats.title: Seismometers on six continents
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Here they are: 158 seismometers on six continents, one reading every fifteen minutes, late 2019 to mid-2020. (touch Brussels) Brussels is this one, in Uccle. Holidays and lockdown are set aside, which leaves 17,027 ordinary days to learn from. So whose recordings are these?
beats.screen: The live research map, 158 dots (if it hasn't loaded in 5 s, the globe clip plays instead). Touch Brussels with one finger: its card shows the network and its DOI.

beats.title: Where every recording comes from
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Every recording has an owner. The 2019 to 2020 recordings are Lecocq and colleagues' published data. (Next) Everything since, 2019 to today, comes from EarthScope's public noise spectra; the earthquakes from the US Geological Survey's catalogue; and holidays and weekends from public calendars, never from the shaking itself. (Next) Behind them are 59 seismic networks, and 54 have a DOI you can cite. On the website, click any station and it shows its network and DOI.

beats.title: Two kinds of shaking
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Not all shaking is us. Here's the coast. The slow wobbles, one every few seconds, are the ocean: waves hitting coasts hundreds of kilometres away, day and night, weekday or weekend. The fast ones, several a second, are engines, wheels and feet. Those small, quick ripples are the ones that carry the week.

beats.screen: The clip plays by itself: “Two kinds of shaking”, the coast. It stops on “Slow: ocean waves…” with big blue rings.
presses: Stops on “Fast: engines, wheels and feet” with small orange rings from the cars

beats.title: The sea keeps no office hours
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.source: R12 data, Brussels (BE.UCC), Oct 2025 – Sep 2026, EarthScope MUSTANG
beats.notes: Held still. Left, the ocean: 11 a.m. and 3 a.m. are almost the same line; the sea doesn't keep office hours. Right, 4 to 14 hertz: daytime is about forty times stronger than night. That gap is us, so that's the band we listen to.
beats.screen: A still: the spectrum, the sea band against the people band.

beats.title: The sea band can't read the week
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: And we tested it. Same model, same days, five bands. The ocean band reads weekday vs weekend 51% of the time: a coin toss. Every band where people are scores above 95%, and the people band, 4 to 14 hertz, is best: almost 99%. Shraddha, how does a model listen?
beats.screen: A still: five bands; the sea band is a coin toss, the people band almost 99%.

beats.title: From the ground to a guess
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: Before going into the details, here's our entire method in six steps. First, we prepare the data: each day becomes one row, we use the 4 to 14 hertz band, remove faulty readings and convert the times to local time. Then we create 25 features. Next, we add labels using public calendars for weekends and holidays. Only ordinary days are used for training. (Next) The model is a Random Forest with 100 decision trees that vote on the day. We test it using entire weeks it hasn't seen before. (Next) Finally, the model's unusual predictions help us identify days that don't follow normal patterns. The next slides explain these steps in more detail.
beats.screen: Row 1: Steps 1–3 (one row per day, 25 features, calendar labels).
presses: Steps 4–5: random forest, honest testing
Step 6: unusual days

beats.title: One day becomes 25 numbers
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: Let's look more closely at the first few steps. Here's one real day's readings. The model can't directly understand a graph, so we convert each day into 25 numbers. Then a logarithm. City shaking spans huge ranges, so the log puts a quiet night and a busy day on one scale. Twenty-four numbers show how active the city was during each hour. This is called the shape. One more number shows how loud the entire day was compared with that station's usual activity. This is called the level. So each day becomes 25 numbers. Every station is different, so looking at the daily shape helps us compare their activity patterns.

beats.screen: The clip plays by itself: one real day's readings on a table. It stops on “3. One number per hour”.

beats.title: A hundred trees vote
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: The next step is the Random Forest. It uses 100 decision trees, and each tree asks a series of simple yes-or-no questions. For example, at six in the morning, was the ground still quiet compared with the rest of the day? If yes, that might point towards a weekend. One tree can be fooled, so we grow a hundred. Each one learns from a random slice of days, and asks its own few yes-or-no questions. Here's a real Wednesday from Brussels that the model hadn't seen before. 97 out of 100 trees correctly say it's a weekday, but they don't all agree on which weekday it is. Only 5 say Wednesday. Weekday or weekend is easy; the exact day is much harder.

beats.screen: The clip plays by itself: one real tree and its first question. It stops on “yes: mostly weekends / no: mostly weekdays”.
presses: The grove grows: “A hundred trees, each from a random slice of days”
The trees vote: the tally fills in, “97 of 100 say weekday”
Ends on “But only 5 say Wednesday…”

beats.title: Graded only on weeks it never saw
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: The final step is testing the model. We never test it on weeks it has already learned from. Monday and Tuesday can have very similar patterns, so we keep entire weeks together and test using five different splits. We also use balanced accuracy, so a model that always predicts weekday doesn't get an unfair score of around 71%. Instead, it gets 50%. Aadit, how did it do?
beats.screen: A still: the calendar of weeks, each shade one round's hidden weeks.

beats.title: How one guess is made
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: Brussels (BE.UCC), Wednesday 15 January 2020; forest trained only on other weeks (forest.json)
beats.notes: So how does the model actually make a prediction? Let's take a day it hasn't seen before: Wednesday, 15 January 2020, in Brussels. We give the model its 25 numbers: 24 describing the day's shape and one showing its overall level. (Next) Each of the 100 trees asks its own yes-or-no questions and gives one vote. These are the actual votes: 31 for Friday, 25 for Tuesday, 23 for Monday, only 5 for Wednesday, and 3 for the weekend. (Next) So the model predicts Friday, which is wrong. But 97 out of 100 trees agree that it's a weekday, which is correct. This shows that the model is much better at identifying weekdays and weekends than telling the exact weekday. Aadit, what does the model look at?
beats.screen: The day's 25 numbers → 100 trees.
presses: The real votes appear: Mon 23, Tue 25, Wed 5, Thu 13, Fri 31, Sat 3, Sun 0
The two answers: “Which day? Friday. Wrong” and “Weekday or weekend? Weekday. Right”

beats.title: What the model looks at
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Brussels, all 115 ordinary days; scikit-learn feature_importances_ (impurity decrease); ml.json
beats.notes: Which of the 25 numbers does the forest lean on? This is Brussels. Each bar is how much that number helps the trees split the days. (Next) The tallest: midnight, one in the afternoon, and six in the morning. Our reading: six a.m. asks whether the city has woken up yet. And the level, how loud the whole day was, ranks only tenth. The shape of the day is what carries the week.
beats.screen: 25 grey bars: how much each number helps.
presses: The top three hours turn black (00:00, 06:00, 13:00), and the line “the level ranks 10 of 25”

beats.title: Where it gets it wrong
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Out-of-fold guesses: Brussels, GroupKFold by week (ml.json); all seismometers, outputs/tables/day_scores.csv
beats.notes: So where does it go wrong? This is a confusion matrix: each row is the real day, each column the model's guess, and the diagonal is right. Brussels, 115 ordinary days, each guessed by a model that never saw its week. (Next) Two blocks. Weekdays blur into each other: a Tuesday is often called a Monday. But the weekend stands apart: right 28 times out of 32, and a weekday is called a weekend only once in 83 days. (Next) And it's not just Brussels: across all 149 seismometers, 16,554 days, the same two blocks. That's why weekday-or-weekend is our headline, and the exact day is the hard part.
beats.screen: Brussels' 7×7 confusion matrix, in counts.
presses: The two blocks are outlined (weekdays orange, weekend blue) with three lines underneath
The second matrix: all 149 seismometers, in %

beats.title: It reads the day
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: One forest per seismometer. Weekday or weekend: 95% in a typical city. The exact day: 47%, where guessing gets 14. In three of the emptiest places in the data, a mountain, the Kalahari, the tip of Chile, it's near chance. No people, no rhythm. And the shape matters: loudness alone names the exact day 30% of the time; with the shape, 47%.
beats.screen: A still: 95% weekday or weekend, 47% exact day; every seismometer as a dot.

beats.title: Its mistakes find holidays
beats.speaker: Aradhya, Aadit
beats.notes: [Aradhya] Back to Christmas. Here's Brussels' whole calendar, one square per day. Christmas was a Wednesday the model had never seen, and it said Sunday. And not just in Brussels: the models at 71% of seismometers did the same. Here are two towers. On weekday holidays it never saw, it said weekend 76% of the time. On ordinary weekdays, only 5%. That gap is the whole point: it learned how people behave, not the calendar. [Aadit] So we turn that into a score: how surprised was the model? One minus the chance it gave the real day. Rank every day by it, and the holidays float to the top. And it holds across the network: this surprise score beats a standard unusual-day alarm in 110 of 147 cities. No holiday labels went into it, and it never trained on these days; the model's own mistakes find them. Here is how that works, step by step.

presses: Stops on the two towers: holidays it never saw against ordinary weekdays
Stops on “Confusion = 1 − P(the real day). Brussels' most surprising days”
Ends on “Better than a standard unusual-day alarm in 110 of 147 cities”

beats.title: From a mistake to an alarm
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Results 7 and 8; groundtruth/detect.py (95th percentile of out-of-fold ordinary days)
beats.notes: How does a mistake become an alarm? Follow Christmas through the boxes. A day it never saw: a Wednesday. The forest says Sunday, and gives Wednesday no chance at all. (Next) So how surprised is it? One minus the chance it gave the real day: one, the maximum. (Next) Then compare that with ordinary days: ninety-five out of a hundred are less surprising than this line. Above the line, flag it. No labels, no list of holidays. Across every seismometer, that alarm beat the standard unusual-day alarm at 110 of 147. We never built a holiday detector. We taught it normal.
beats.screen: Boxes 1–2: a new day (Christmas 2019) → the forest guesses Sunday.
presses: Box 3: surprise = 1.00
Boxes 4–5: above 95% of ordinary days → flag it; then 76% and 110 of 147

beats.title: It recognises rest, not the name of the day
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: A model trained on all the other cities still reads a new one: 83%. Trained only on Saturday-Sunday countries, it calls Salfit's Fridays weekend: it recognises rest, not the name of the day. Jeddah, our third Friday city, didn't transfer. And when the UAE moved its weekend in 2022, we wrote the prediction down before downloading anything: Sundays got 20% quieter, luck would do that about 3 times in 1,000. One sensor, 90 km from Sharjah city, and Fridays got 53% busier, which we didn't predict.
beats.screen: A still: the weekend moves (Salfit and the UAE).

beats.title: The dare, done properly
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.source: Result 19 (docs/17) and the second-by-second test (docs/20), both written down before running
beats.notes: Last time we made a dare. Here's rush hour: every car on this street shaking the ground at once. Now a small earthquake, far away, arrives from below. In all that traffic, it's easy to miss. The dare: if we know what this hour normally sounds like, subtract the people, and find the quake underneath. We tried it first on fifteen-minute averages: 998 against 953, p = 0.053. Not supported, and outside one Puerto Rico swarm a simple rolling median did best. A quake lasts seconds; fifteen minutes blurs it away. So we wrote a proper test down in advance: second-by-second recordings, years the first test never touched, at most 100 quakes per station so no swarm decides it. Result: with the people subtracted, 413 found; the raw recording, 501. Not supported: it made things worse. A plain rolling baseline of the last five minutes did best, 524. A city's weekly rhythm is the right model for reading the day, and the wrong one for finding a quake that lasts seconds. Detecting quakes that happened; never predicting them. Shraddha, what else didn't work?

beats.title: What didn't work
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: There were also a few things that didn't work as expected. During lockdowns, weekdays didn't simply start looking like Sundays. Only about a quarter were classified as weekends; many looked different from any day the model had learned. Our shape-and-level features also didn't perform better than using the raw hourly readings, although they gave us a simpler way to compare stations. And the original dataset covers only one season and uses national holidays. So what happens when we use data from more years?
beats.screen: A still: three things that didn't work.

beats.title: Now scale it
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.source: Results 15–17, Jan 2019 – Sep 2026, 33 cities, EarthScope MUSTANG
beats.notes: We went back to the source: seven years, every station from the study that is still recording and publicly served, plus Sharjah. 33 cities, 72,000 ordinary days. This is a new, bigger model: three frequency bands, every half hour, gradient boosting, still tested only on weeks it never saw. A new experiment, so new numbers.
beats.screen: A still: 33 cities, 7 years, the ordinary days.

beats.title: More data helps, then flattens
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: Results 16–18, 2019–26, 33 cities, every score on weeks the model never saw
beats.notes: We might expect seven years of data to make the model much better. For weekday versus weekend classification, it reaches 97%. But exact-day accuracy only increases from 38% with 100 days of data to 57% with all the data, and then improvement slows down. Training one model on all 33 cities together actually performs worse in every city. This is because a Tuesday can sound different from one city to another. But when we give the model the full week around a day instead of just that day, accuracy reaches 96%.
beats.screen: A still: the learning curve from 100 days to all of them, and 96% for the week.

beats.title: Everything we built
beats.speaker: Aradhya
beats.notes: Everything you've seen runs on one website, built from these same files. Two sources of data, one set of Python code, and a GitHub Action every morning. (Next) The pages to explore: a two-minute tour; the globe, any day since 2019; Ask, the model's guess for any day; and the research map, every seismometer scored. (Next) And the pages that keep going: City Pulse, which scores yesterday every night; a game where you try to beat the model; and pages that explain how it works and where it stops. The front page first.

beats.title: What runs every night
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.notes: So how does the website get information about what happened the previous day? Let's follow the steps. Seismometers record vibrations throughout the day. EarthScope makes the data available about two days later. Every morning at six, a GitHub Action automatically downloads the latest available data. (Next) Two models then analyse each day: one is a fixed model trained on one year of data, which stays unchanged. The other is a learning model that makes a prediction first and then learns from that day. (Next) The results are saved in the GitHub repository and published through Vercel, where the globe, Ask and City Pulse pages can use them. The seven-year models in Ask are trained separately on a laptop and saved in the same way. Let's see it running.
beats.screen: Seismometers → EarthScope → GitHub Action.
presses: Frozen model and learning model
Saved in git → the website, and the “built once on a laptop” line

beats.title: City Pulse: every night
beats.speaker: Shraddha
beats.source: City Pulse, pre-registered in docs/19, interim
beats.notes: Here it is: City Pulse. Every night, it shows the previous day's results for each city, including what the model predicted and whether it was correct. (Next → the learning card) Further down, we can see the fixed model and the learning model side by side. Does learning from more data actually help? We prepared a test before writing the code. Based on our earlier results, we don't expect a huge improvement because accuracy had already started to level off. The final result will be available in January, so these are still early results. (Next → the predictions board) Finally, the predictions board shows predictions saved in the repository before the actual day, with the real results added afterwards. Aradhya, one more page.

beats.title: Still useless?
beats.speaker: Aadit
beats.notes: So, back to where we started. Seismologists call this shaking noise, and throw it away. Still useless? There's a network already buried under many of the world's cities, recording for decades, free. It hears a neighbourhood, not a person: no phones, no cameras. And ours is running tonight. Everyone measures how loud the ground is. We taught a model what normal sounds like, and its mistakes tell us when something happened. That's GroundTruth. Thank you.
